_note: Narration script for the AO module 'Bushfire and burnover' (PRO-239 v2.6, PRO-082 v3.5, SAAS EMAP presentation V3.0). Lee on eleven_v4, [calmly] prefix, two takes (scenes 1-4, then 5-8). The prompt spelled ABC, EOC, CFS, GRN, PPE as letters, P2 'P two' and 1485 AM 'fourteen eighty-five A M'; captions use the text here.

lines.head: Fire country
sentences: Bushfire country is where we live and work.
You might be on standby at a staging area.
You might be treating someone hurt by the fire.
Or you might just be driving home from a job.
A burnover is when a fast fire front overtakes people and vehicles.
The best protection is not being there.
But if it happens, you need to know what to do.

lines.head: Read the day
sentences: Start with the Fire Danger Rating.
It doesn't tell you how likely a fire is.
It tells you how bad one would be.
Moderate.
Plan and prepare.
High.
Be ready to act.
Extreme.
Take action now.
Catastrophic.
For your survival, leave bushfire risk areas.
Listen to your local ABC radio for warnings.
On the Eyre Peninsula, that's 1485 AM.

lines.head: Ready for a fire day
sentences: On an Extreme or Catastrophic day, check your vehicle.
Burnover kit.
Helmets.
P2 masks.
Plenty of water.
At least three-quarters of a tank of fuel.
No burnover kit?
Tell your Operations Manager or Team Leader at the start of the shift.

lines.head: Responding in
sentences: The EOC directs every response into a known fire area.
Often the CFS brings patients out to a safe staging area.
You don't go onto an active fireground without a fire appliance escort.
Going in?
All lights on, and find a place to turn around.
Park on burnt ground if you can.
And if there's any doubt, don't go in.
Call the EOC.

lines.head: A burnover is coming
sentences: If a burnover is coming, don't try to outrun it.
Look for a building close by.
If there isn't one, stay in the vehicle.
Long blasts on the siren or horn bring everyone back.
Park off the road, in the clearest spot, facing the fire.

lines.head: Before it hits
sentences: Press the GRN emergency button.
Your call sign, and MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY.
Give your Garmin coordinates.
Windows and vents shut.
Engine off.
Air conditioner off.
Headlights, hazards and beacons on.
Gloves, P2 mask and goggles from the kit.

lines.head: Get low
sentences: Get into the back, below window level, beside the airway seat.
Get under the woollen fire blanket.
Cover your patient with blankets, and offer them a mask.
Drink water, but don't pour it on yourself.
It'll be loud, hot and frightening.
Look after each other.
Stay inside until the sound of the fire has passed.

lines.head: After the front
sentences: Then get out carefully, with your helmet and PPE on.
If the doors won't open, break a side or back window.
Not the windscreen.
Check everyone for injuries.
Call the EOC, and move to burnt ground.
A medical officer will check you before anyone decides about the rest of your shift.
Know the day.
Know your kit.
Know the drill.
